theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit
doctrine: The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit
summary: The Spirit’s personhood, deity, procession, and his work in conviction, regeneration, indwelling, sealing, sanctifying
readingInstruction: Read John 14:15-31, John 16:5-15, and Acts 2:1-21. Today is a doctrinal pause on the Holy Spirit: who he is and what he does. Notice what Jesus promised, and what happened at Pentecost.
settingTheScene: On the night before his death, Jesus promised his disciples another Helper. Fifty days after the resurrection, on the Jewish feast of Pentecost, that promise came true. The Spirit had been at work in the Old Testament, hovering over creation, empowering prophets and craftsmen, and anointing kings. But Pentecost marks the beginning of a new stage: the Spirit poured out on all God’s people, as the new covenant promised. The church has confessed the Holy Spirit as the third person of the Trinity, equal with the Father and the Son.
observation: “And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16-17).
“But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14:26).
“And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment” (John 16:8).
“When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth” (John 16:13).
“He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16:14).
“And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting” (Acts 2:2).
“And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:4).
“And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Acts 2:17).
doctrinalFocus: The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity: fully God, one in being with the Father and the Son, yet distinct as a person. Jesus calls him “he” and “the Helper” (the Greek word, paraclete, means one called alongside to help, advocate, or comfort). The Bible gives the Spirit divine attributes (eternal, all-knowing, present everywhere) and divine works (creation, inspiration of Scripture, new birth). His work in salvation is to apply what Christ has accomplished. He convicts of sin, gives new birth, unites believers to Christ, dwells within them, seals them, sanctifies them, gives gifts for the building up of the church, and assures them that they are God’s children. His ministry is Christ-centered: Jesus said, “He will glorify me.” At Pentecost, the Spirit was poured out on all believers, not just prophets and kings, as Joel foretold. Every Christian has the Spirit (Romans 8:9), and every Christian is called to be filled with him continually (Ephesians 5:18). Christians differ on the nature of some gifts, such as tongues and healing, and on whether the experience called the baptism or filling of the Spirit is distinct from conversion. All agree that without the Spirit there is no new life, no understanding of Scripture, and no power for witness.
interpretation:
In the Upper Room, Jesus tells his troubled disciples that he is leaving, but they will not be left as orphans. He will ask the Father, and the Father will give “another Helper.” The word “another” means another of the same kind. The Spirit will be to them what Jesus has been. And he will be with them forever. He is called the Spirit of truth. He will dwell with them and in them. He will teach them and remind them of what Jesus said. This is the promise behind the New Testament: the Spirit would help the apostles to remember and understand what Jesus taught, and so give us the Scriptures.

In chapter 16, Jesus says it is to their advantage that he goes away, for the Helper will not come otherwise. The Spirit’s work in the world is to convict: of sin, because they do not believe in Jesus; of righteousness, because Jesus goes to the Father and the world no longer sees him; and of judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. His work with believers is to guide them into all truth, and above all to glorify Christ. He does not speak on his own authority. A mark of the Spirit’s presence is that Jesus is exalted.

Then on the day of Pentecost, the promise comes. A sound like a rushing wind fills the house. Tongues like flames rest on each of them. They are all filled with the Holy Spirit and speak in other languages, so that visitors from many nations each hear “the mighty works of God” in their own tongue. Some mock, saying they are drunk. Peter stands and quotes Joel: “In the last days, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy.” The reversal of Babel has begun. At Babel languages were confused and people scattered. At Pentecost, languages are understood and people gathered. The Spirit comes on young and old, men and women, slave and free, so that the whole people of God can know him. This is the new covenant: not a few prophets but a kingdom of prophets.
connection: Genesis 1:2 and Psalm 104:30 show the Spirit in creation. Numbers 11:29 has Moses wishing all the LORD’s people were prophets. Ezekiel 36:26-27 and Jeremiah 31:33-34 promised the Spirit in the new covenant. Joel 2:28-32 is Peter’s text. Genesis 11:1-9 is Babel. Romans 8:9-16 describes the Spirit in the believer. Ephesians 1:13-14 and 5:18 speak of the seal and the filling. Galatians 5:22-23 lists the fruit of the Spirit. 1 Corinthians 12 to 14 treat gifts.
application:
Thank the Father for the Spirit by name, and ask him to fill you today.

Notice where Jesus is being glorified in your life, a sign of the Spirit’s work.

Ask the Spirit to open your Bible as you read, as Jesus promised.
prayerPrompts: Thank the Father for sending the Spirit to be with you forever.
Ask the Spirit to teach you, convict you, and remind you of Jesus.
Tell him where you need his help today.
